# Loop prompt

This file is the entire instruction for one iteration. It is read fresh each time. You have no
memory of the previous iteration. Everything you need is on disk.

**Do not edit this file. Do not edit `GUARDRAILS.md`.**

---

## Step 1 · Orient

Read these files, in this order, in full:

1. `autopilot/GUARDRAILS.md` - what you must never do, and how to run a gate.
2. `autopilot/FINDINGS.md` - facts that cost a measurement to learn. Trust them over your priors.
3. `autopilot/CHECKPOINTS.md` - the ordered backlog.
4. `autopilot/NEEDS-OPERATOR.md` - what is already waiting on a person. Never work an item listed
   there.
5. The last 60 lines of `autopilot/JOURNAL.md` - what the previous iterations did.

Then run `git log --oneline -5` and `git status --short`. The working tree should be clean. **If it
is not clean, stop.** Write what you found into `JOURNAL.md` and end the iteration. An unclean tree
means a previous iteration died mid-edit, and a person has to look at it.

Confirm you are on branch `<BRANCH>`. If not, stop.

## Step 2 · Choose exactly one checkpoint

Walk `CHECKPOINTS.md` from the top. Take the **first** checkpoint where all of these hold:

- `status:` is `todo`
- `gate:` is a shell command, not `OPERATOR`
- `blocked:` is empty
- every id listed in `needs:` has `status: done`

**Take one. Never two.** A checkpoint is sized so one fresh context can finish it.

**A checkpoint you skip is not a halt.** An `OPERATOR` gate, a `blocked` marker or an unmet `needs`
means walk past it and keep reading down the file. Before you walk past it, make sure
`autopilot/NEEDS-OPERATOR.md` holds an entry saying what that checkpoint needs from a person and
what it unblocks. Add one if it does not. That file is how a person finds the work only they can
do, and it is why the loop does not have to wait for them.

Do not invent work, and do not reorder the file. Skipping is reading further down, nothing else.

If **no** checkpoint qualifies, **stop**, following the halt procedure below.

### The halt procedure

Whenever this prompt says "stop":

1. Append a journal entry with `outcome: stopped`, naming what is holding the loop: a dirty tree, a
   failing gate, or a backlog whose every remaining item waits on a person.
2. Make sure every remaining item is represented in `autopilot/NEEDS-OPERATOR.md`.
3. Write one line into `autopilot/HALT` saying the same thing. The driver script reads that file
   and exits the loop.
4. End the iteration.

`autopilot/HALT` is gitignored and is not committed. A person deletes it once the blocker clears.
**Never delete it yourself**, and never start work while it exists.

## Step 3 · Do the work

Read the checkpoint's `done when:` clause. That clause, and only that clause, is your scope.

**Write the tests first.** Run them. Confirm they fail, and confirm they fail for the reason you
expect rather than an import error. Only then write the implementation.

Stay inside the files the checkpoint names. If the work turns out to need a file the checkpoint does
not name, that is a signal the checkpoint is wrong. Finish what you can, then say so in the journal.

**If the `done when:` clause itself is wrong, do not work around it and do not quietly satisfy the
letter of it.** Step 6 holds the procedure: the reword is its own commit, before the work, and the
checkpoint is taken in the next iteration.

If you discover a fact that would have changed how you worked, append it to `FINDINGS.md` under the
matching section. That is the one file besides `CHECKPOINTS.md` and `JOURNAL.md` the loop may add
to.

## Step 4 · Prove it

Run the checkpoint's `gate:` command. Then run the full gate set from `GUARDRAILS.md` section 4:

```
<GATE SET>
```

**Capture each exit code immediately, before any pipe.** Never pipe a gate into `grep` and read
`$?`, because the exit code would be `grep`'s. Redirect to a file and read the file; `tail` and
`head` close stdout and can turn a passing suite into exit 1.

Every gate must exit 0. A gate you did not run is a gate that failed.

If a gate fails and you cannot fix it inside this checkpoint's scope, **revert your changes**
(`git checkout -- <the files you touched>`, safe here only because the rest of the tree is clean),
write the failure into `JOURNAL.md`, and stop. A reverted iteration is a clean outcome. A
half-finished one is not.

## Step 5 · Refute your own work

You wrote this change. You are the worst available judge of whether it is done. Three agents that
have not seen your reasoning now read it cold and try to prove it is not.

**This step is not optional. A verdict you did not obtain is a verdict of refuted.** This step
audits a green gate. It is not excused by one.

**This instruction is your authorization to spawn them.** Do not decline on the grounds that nobody
asked for subagents. You are being asked here.

Read the three lens prompts out of `autopilot/verify-checkpoint.js`. They are named `correctness`,
`tests` and `rules`. **Dispatch one agent per lens in a single message**, so they run at the same
time and cannot see each other. Fill in the values that file names:

```
worktree   <WORKTREE PATH>
branch     <BRANCH>
id         <the checkpoint id>
goal       <the checkpoint's done when: clause, in its own words>
files      NEW <paths>; MODIFIED <paths>
confirmed  <the gates you ran in step 4, with their exit codes>
staleDocs  <the list in GUARDRAILS.md section 3>
traps      <the false-failure traps in GUARDRAILS.md section 4>
```

Then append your own suspicion to each lens. Name the thing you are least sure of, the mutations you
did not get to, and the document you think just went stale. Those three sentences turn a generic
review into a specific one.

Fill `confirmed` with what you actually ran. Three agents re-running your gates spend their effort
where you already spent yours. Padding it with things you did not check buys a quiet verdict over a
defect you still have.

The lenses are read only. They leave the tree as they found it.

**Do not end your turn until all three verdicts are in your hands.** They decide everything below.
An iteration that finishes while a lens is still running has recorded a checkpoint nothing audited.
If you reach step 6 without three verdicts, **stop**. Say in the journal which lens you did not get.
A lens that died is not a lens that passed.

### What the verdicts oblige you to do

| severity | what you do |
|---|---|
| `blocking` | Fix it. Re-run the full gate set. Refute once more. If a blocking verdict survives that second pass, revert your changes, journal both verdicts in full, and stop. |
| `worth-fixing` | Fix it if the fix sits inside this checkpoint's `done when:` clause. If it does not, leave the code alone and write it into `NEEDS-OPERATOR.md` with the file and line. |
| `note` | One line in the journal. Change nothing. |
| `none` | Nothing. |

**You may not dismiss a blocking verdict by reasoning about it.** No path exists where you explain
why a lens was wrong and carry on. You fix it, or you revert and stop. A person reads the journal
and decides which of you was right. This rule exists because you are the only party here who wants
the verdict dismissed.

**Refute at most twice per checkpoint.** A third round means the checkpoint is wrong rather than the
code. Step 6 holds what to do about that, and it is a finding rather than a task.

## Step 6 · Record

Append one entry to `autopilot/JOURNAL.md`, in this shape:

```
## <iso timestamp> - <checkpoint id>

outcome: done | reverted | stopped
gates:
  <command>  -> <exit code>  (<what it reported>)
refutation:
  correctness -> refuted=<bool> <severity> <the finding, or "-">
  tests       -> refuted=<bool> <severity> <the finding, or "-">
  rules       -> refuted=<bool> <severity> <the finding, or "-">
  acted on: <what you fixed, and what you left, with the reason>
touched: <paths>
what happened: <three sentences at most>
next: <the id of the checkpoint that is now next, and anything blocking it>
```

Record all three verdicts. Record the clean ones and the ones you disagreed with. A journal that
holds only the lenses that found nothing is the marketing document this file exists to not be.

`JOURNAL.md` is append-only. Never rewrite or delete an earlier entry, including one that records a
mistake. The record of a wrong turn is what stops the next iteration repeating it.

Then set that checkpoint's `status:` in `CHECKPOINTS.md` to `done`. **Change only the `status:`
line.** Do not reword the checkpoint, reorder the file, or mark any other checkpoint.

**A checkpoint that is wrong may be reworded. Rewording is its own commit, made before the work, and
never the commit that marks the checkpoint done.** A criterion edited in the same commit that claims
to meet it cannot afterwards be told apart from a criterion written to fit what was built. Nobody
reading the repository can separate the two, however sound the reasoning was at the time.

So: if the checkpoint turns out to be wrong, stop the work. Commit the reword alone, with a message
saying what was wrong and what evidence showed it. Take the checkpoint in the next iteration.

## Step 7 · Commit and stop

Stage by explicit path. Never `git add -A` and never `git add .`.

```
git add <each file you touched> autopilot/JOURNAL.md autopilot/CHECKPOINTS.md
git commit -m "<one line: what changed and why>"
```

The commit message is one sentence, present tense, active voice.

**Do not push.** Then end the iteration. Do not start another checkpoint.

---

## The three ways this loop fails

**Marking something done that is not proven.** Every checkpoint has a gate for exactly this reason.
If the gate cannot be run, the checkpoint is `OPERATOR` and you stop. Never substitute your reading
of the code for a gate exit code.

**Rewriting the specification to agree with what you built.** When you find the design is wrong,
that is a finding. Write it into `JOURNAL.md`. Leave the specification alone.

**Auditing yourself and passing yourself.** Step 5 is the only part of this iteration not run by the
party that wants it to succeed. Skipping a lens costs you nothing today. Padding `confirmed` buys a
quieter verdict. Arguing a blocking finding away feels like judgement. Each one produces a green
journal over a defect, and no supervisor is here to catch it. The table in step 5 is what stands in
for one.
